subjective.question: What is meant by Militant Journalism? Name the prominent journalists of that era.
subjective.answer: Militant Journalism is the name given in the history of the print media of the sub-continent to the brave and bold stance adopted by Muslim journalists against the ferocious press laws of the British government. Despite bans and punishments, these journalists continued to condemn the brutalities of the East India Company and to awaken the people. The prominent names of that era were Maulana Zafar Ali Khan (Zamindar), Maulana Muhammad Ali Johar (Comrade and Hamdard) and Maulana Hasrat Mohani (Urdu-e-Mualla). Zamindar faced several bans but continued to print and gained great popularity among the people.

subjective.question: State the difference between Mob, Mass and Public.
subjective.answer: Mob is a result of an immediate problem; when the problem is over, the mob also disperses. The people in a mob gather quickly without any plan, have no link with each other and no resemblance of income, status or intelligence. Mass means a large number of people who have the same reaction of liking or disliking, but it is not a deliberate effort — for example, one million people reading the same famous daily is a similarity of liking by chance. Public is a group of people that emerges after a deliberate effort; a newspaper builds opinion, so its audience is called public. Public opinion is never unanimous, it must be apparent and expressive, and sometimes even the opinion of a minority prevails as public opinion.

subjective.question: Write a note on the newspaper 'Imroz'.
subjective.answer: Imroz started its publication after independence and, for the first time in Pakistan, collected a very good team under one roof; prominent personalities like Abdullah Malik, Faiz Ahmed Faiz and Chiragh Hassan Hasrat were associated with it, so it very quickly attained a reputable place among the leading newspapers. It was published by Progressive Papers Ltd. Imroz also introduced new trends in newspapers: it hired a woman reporter and started publishing articles on the problems of women under the title “Khatoon ki Nazar Main”, and its features, published along with pictures, gave feature writing a new dimension.

subjective.question: Why did the newspapers shift their focus away from political news during Ayub Khan's era, and what new trends emerged?
subjective.answer: Since 1857 the newspapers of the sub-continent were habitual of keeping their focus on politics, but Ayub Khan's martial law government put a ban on all political news. To maintain the interest of the readers, newspapers started seeking other topics and began publishing different supplements, such as Sports Supplements, Women Supplements and Youth Supplements, so the focus shifted to social life. Imroz introduced women's pages and articles on women's problems, film pages and film bulletins gave rise to glamorous journalism, features began to be printed with pictures, and weekly and episodic features covering social and cultural aspects became popular. In place of political news, official statements of government ministers began to appear in the newspapers.

subjective.question: What were the harsh actions taken by Ayub Khan against international news agencies?
subjective.answer: Ayub Khan's government took a complete hold over all the news resources of the country. The two independent news agencies of Pakistan, APP (Associated Press of Pakistan) and PPI (Pakistan Press International), were taken over by the martial law government. International news agencies were bound that they would not distribute news and reports directly to radio and other newspapers in Pakistan; they were asked to send their news via APP or PPI. This action was taken to control and restrict the news and information coming from international media from reaching the people of Pakistan, and in this way the freedom of press was totally abolished.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of mass media in the 1970 elections and the crisis of 1971.
subjective.answer: In the 1970 elections the mass media did not perform an impartial role. The government-owned National Press Trust papers favoured the rightists and gave the impression that they would easily win, while in fact the Awami League won in East Pakistan and the PPP in West Pakistan; only the newspaper 'Azad' presented a fair and realistic picture. Newspapers reported rumours, speculations and mutual accusations of treason instead of informing the people about the real changes taking place in East Pakistan. When the National Assembly session was postponed and the Awami League launched the non-cooperation movement on 7th March, the papers simply portrayed the government stance that “everything is fine”. The language barrier — only English was a common source of communication between the two wings — further hindered understanding. By keeping the people uninformed, the media failed in its duty, and the crisis ended in the separation of East Pakistan.

subjective.question: What problems did Pakistan face after the fall of Dhaka, and what role did the media play in that era?
subjective.answer: After the separation of East Pakistan, Pakistan faced many problems: a pessimistic approach of the people, an economic crisis and a tarnished reputation in the community of nations, and there was dead silence on the political arena. Indian mass media propagated that the Two Nation Theory had failed, and Indira Gandhi said it was “buried in the Bay of Bengal”. In this scenario the newspapers of Pakistan played a very positive and critical role: they encouraged the people, gave them self-belief and splendidly defended the stance that the separation was a political failure, not the failure of the ideology of Pakistan. The media also portrayed the feelings of the Muslim Ummah very positively during the Second Islamic Conference at Lahore in 1974, which helped Pakistan regain its prominent position in the Islamic world.

subjective.question: Write down the three demands of Zia-ul-Haq from the USA to play a basic role in the era of the 1979 Afghan crisis.
subjective.answer: General Zia-ul-Haq presented three demands to perform a basic role in the Afghan crisis: (a) the arms supply given to the Mujahideen should be of Russian origin and no American ammunition would be used; (b) no other country, including the USA, would be allowed to contact the Mujahideen directly, and aid for the Afghan refugees would be dealt through Pakistan, so that Pakistan could avoid any chaotic condition; and (c) at a given time, two aeroplanes loaded with ammunition would land in Pakistan, and further arms supply would be made after confirmation by this country. The Americans agreed to all three demands.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of media during Zia-ul-Haq's regime.
subjective.answer: Zia-ul-Haq imposed the third martial law on 5th July 1977. During his regime the declarations of many newspapers were cancelled — Musawat, the party newspaper of the PPP, was the first target — and 18 magazines and newspapers were closed down while almost 150 journalists were arrested and punished by martial law courts. Pre-censorship was imposed for a long time and newspapers protested by leaving blank spaces for censored news. The PFUJ started a movement against these censorship policies. On the Afghan issue, all newspapers covered Afghan stories and fully supported the Mujahidin and the Jihadi groups, favouring the holy war against communism; however, the media did not mention the negative aspects of the Afghan policy, such as sectarian violence and religious extremism. Pakistani papers also began to think that religion is a sensitive issue and avoided touching it in editorials and articles.

subjective.question: What was the reason for publishing the Hamood Ur Rahman Commission Report after 34 years?
subjective.answer: The Hamood Ur Rahman Commission Report was the inquiry report of the fall of Dhaka. It remained unpublished for 34 years and was finally published in 2005. The reason was that an Indian website revealed and published the report on the internet; when it became an open secret, the government of Pakistan also decided to publicize the report. It is the best example of how the international scenario affects national policies.

subjective.question: Discuss the work of newspapers on the decision of Musharraf's government to support the US after 9/11.
subjective.answer: After 9/11, the blame was put on Osama bin Laden and the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the USA decided on the military option. Iran had no bilateral relations with the US, so Pakistan was the last suitable option, and President Musharraf answered in affirmation regarding help to the US forces. Pakistani newspapers clearly wrote that the people of Pakistan did not like President Musharraf's stand on the Afghan issue, and some newspapers even wrote that the US is not a reliable friend of Pakistan. At the same time, Musharraf's statements that terrorism cannot be eradicated unless its root causes are removed were also given space, so a balanced sort of view was seen in the newspapers — they presented the feelings of the government as well as some anti-government feelings.

subjective.question: Discuss the condition of newspapers in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: In Pakistan the mainstream newspapers are either English or Urdu newspapers, while local-language newspapers have not much area of influence. The readership of English and Urdu newspapers differs greatly in culture, values, status, economic interest and political understanding, and the two often have very different policies — for example on religious extremism, child labour and women's rights, which English newspapers deal with seriously while Urdu newspapers remain largely silent. Much of the newspaper staff is untrained, because the mushroom growth of newspapers after RPPO could not find technically competent staff, so many journalists are unaware of working conditions and the ethics of journalism. Dummy newspapers also exist, which keep their declarations intact by submitting only a few copies to the press branch.

subjective.question: What are the English and Urdu newspaper policies regarding religious extremism?
subjective.answer: English and Urdu newspapers in Pakistan have very different policies on religious extremism. Religious extremism is condemned by English newspapers, while Urdu newspapers have no such policy; in fact, many times articles were written or news was moulded in Urdu newspapers in such a way that people developed sympathy with religious extremists all around the world. Urdu newspapers give about 70% of their news in the form of political statements, and the politicians also did not condemn religious extremism. This is the basic reason why President Musharraf's policy to uproot extremism could not succeed — the majority Urdu newspapers never supported the policy, while English newspapers played their part.

subjective.question: What are the basic three essential parts of a newspaper nowadays?
subjective.answer: Nowadays a newspaper has three basic segments: (a) Advertising, (b) Editorial and (c) News (reporting). Advertising is the life blood of a newspaper because newspapers depend on multinational advertisers for their revenue. The editorial page carries the subjective opinion — editorials, columns and letters to the editor — and usually reflects the policy of the newspaper, while news must remain objective. Reporting is the third segment: every kind of news is classified into its respective beat, every reporter has a special beat, and news is constantly monitored by sub-editors in the newsroom in three shifts.

subjective.question: What importance does the editorial have in a newspaper? Write what you know about the editorial page.
subjective.answer: The editorial is the subjective opinion of the newspaper on the important issues of the day. The ethics of journalism say that news should be objective, therefore a separate page is reserved for opinion and it is called the editorial page. Usually the editorial page reflects the policy of the newspaper. Columns are also printed on the editorial page — in the beginning columns were just humorous, and prominent columnists of the sub-continent include Abdul Majeed Salik, Chiragh Hassan Hasrat and Atta-ul-Haq Qasmi. Columns are usually called the interpretation of the news. Letters to the editor also carry personal opinion, so they are printed on the editorial page as well.

subjective.question: Define Magazine, Periodical and Journal.
subjective.answer: A magazine is a periodical publication containing a wide variety of articles on various subjects. A periodical is a regular issue from a press; it could be a magazine or a review. A journal is a professional periodical. The term 'magazine' was first used in 1731 in the title of “Gentleman's Magazine”, founded in London.

subjective.question: Is the introduction of forum discussion beneficial and attractive to readers?
subjective.answer: Yes, forum discussion is a new and beneficial trend in our newspapers. Papers invite different experts on an issue, which gives the advantage of having different opinions at one platform, and these discussions are then published in the newspapers. It is a healthy and informative source for the public because readers get expert and diverse viewpoints on serious issues in one place. Many newspapers also organize seminars and discussion panels on serious issues, such as the Hudood Ordinance, which enhances the freedom of expression and attracts readers.

subjective.question: Discuss whether feature writing is helpful for a newspaper or not.
subjective.answer: Feature writing is very helpful for a newspaper. In Pakistan there is no investigative reporting, and features have covered the gap of investigative reporting. There is a wide difference between news and a feature: features are not time-bound while news is time-bound, and features can be objective and subjective while news is always objective. Feature writers take their material from the happenings around them. In Ayub's era, when political news was banned, features got a new dimension — features along with pictures were printed, and weekly and episodic features covered the social and cultural aspects of life, keeping the readers' interest intact in the newspapers.

subjective.question: Why are newspapers subdued to the policies of multinationals?
subjective.answer: Advertising is a very important feature and the life blood of a newspaper. There is a general concept that news sources are directly under the control of Jews, which is a misconception; Jews in fact own multinational companies and they are the biggest advertisers. Because newspapers depend on these multinational companies for advertising revenue, they subdue to the policies of these multinationals, since the most persuasive advertising leaves a lasting impact and the newspaper cannot afford to lose its advertisers.

subjective.question: Write down a few international news agencies.
subjective.answer: The four major international news agencies are: Reuters (the Reuter Telegram Company of London, 1851, considered the oldest news agency of the world), Associated Press (AP) of America, United Press International (UPI), and Agence France-Presse (AFP) of France. The first international news agencies formed in Europe were Agence Havas of Paris (1835), Reuters of London (1851) and the Continental Telegraphen Compagnie (Wolff Agency) of Berlin (1849). These agencies provide extensive service to their subscribers in more than 150 countries and work 24 hours.

subjective.question: What is the difference between the working of a news agency and a newspaper?
subjective.answer: A newspaper has its own policy under its own specific management, however, a news agency cannot form a specific policy or point of view. A news agency has its clients and subscribers in different parts of the world, each with their own specific policies and stance on different issues; therefore, a news agency is bound to adopt an unbiased, objective and indifferent approach in its reporting and services to keep its subscribers satisfied. News agencies also do not publish the news themselves; they collect news and provide it to newspapers, radio, television and other subscribers.

subjective.question: What do you know about the Rowlatt Act 1919?
subjective.answer: The Rowlatt Act of 1919 was a black law introduced in British India. Under this law, the government got the authority to persecute any Indian, and the arrested person had no facility of legal assistance and no right to appeal — just as the 'Lettres de Cachet' in France before the French Revolution. Quaid-e-Azam resigned from the Central Legislature in protest against this black law.

subjective.question: Write a note on the Press and Publications Ordinance (PPO).
subjective.answer: The Press and Publications Ordinance (PPO) was formed and enforced in 1961 by Ayub Khan's government to keep the newspapers under government control. It was a black law, completely boycotted by media organizations and journalists; according to one of its clauses, all newspapers were ordered to publish the handouts of DPR/PID as they were, which is simply against the freedom of press. In 1963, West Pakistan and East Pakistan Press and Publications Ordinances were introduced, and although pressure resulted in an amendment, its harshness remained the same. After the death of General Zia-ul-Haq in 1988, the caretaker government repealed the PPO and introduced the Registration of Printing Press and Publications Ordinance (RPPPO), after which the press began working in a comparatively better environment.

subjective.question: What do you know about APNS, CPNE and PFUJ?
subjective.answer: These are the three major organizations formed in Pakistan to secure the rights of journalists, newspapers and editors. APNS (All Pakistan Newspapers Society) is the organization of newspaper owners, founded in 1953 by pioneering editors and publishers like Hamid Nizami and Altaf Hussain to protect the rights and commercial interests of newspapers; the Daily Dawn was its founding member. CPNE (Council of Pakistan Newspaper Editors) was established in 1955 as a representative body of the editors of Pakistan's publications; both APNS and CPNE struggled against the black press laws. PFUJ (Pakistan Federal Union of Journalists), set up in 1950 and located in Islamabad, works for a better working environment for journalists and is arguably South Asia's first association representing the journalists of an entire country; it has always stood as a symbol of freedom of speech.

subjective.question: Discuss the people's right to know and the freedom of expression under Article 19.
subjective.answer: Freedom of press is linked with the people's right to know — free access to information that ensures accountability and a true democratic society. Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) states that everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression, including the freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media regardless of frontiers; the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) contains the same right in its Article 19. In Pakistan, Article 19 of the Constitution of 1973 also guarantees freedom of speech, expression and the press, but subject to vague conditions that governments can use to exploit journalists and media organizations. The Freedom of Information Ordinance was promulgated in October 2002 under international donors' pressure, but it has serious flaws, such as prohibiting the making public of important documents like file notings and minutes of meetings.

subjective.question: What is a news agency? Write a note on the news agencies of Pakistan.
subjective.answer: A news agency is an organization that acts as a source of news for different newspapers, radio, television and other organizations and individuals; news agencies do not publish the news themselves but collect it and provide it to their subscribers, and they are also called wire services or press agencies. In Pakistan, the part of the Associated Press of India that remained in Pakistan was declared the first news agency of Pakistan under the name Associated Press of Pakistan (APP); in 1960 Ayub Khan's government took APP under government control and it is still working as a state-owned news agency. In 1956 some journalists parted from APP and formed a private agency, the Pakistan Press Association, which later became Pakistan Press International (PPI). Another agency, United Press of Pakistan (UPP), came into existence in December 1949, founded by Mr. Qutubuddin Aziz as a private limited company.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of mass media during the Afghan War.
subjective.answer: During the Afghan war, Pakistan was given a leading role to stop the communist influence because of its geographical position, and the mass media fully favoured this holy war against communism. All the newspapers of that time covered Afghan stories and fully supported the Mujahidin and Jihadi groups, and Pakistan was used as a base for the militant movement launched in collaboration with General Zia-ul-Haq, which ended in 1989. However, the mass media did not mention the negative aspects of the Afghan policy: militant and sectarian groups in Pakistan got expertise and modern weapons, and religious extremism and sectarian violence were encouraged, while newspapers made no planned effort to discourage sectarian violence.

subjective.question: How did the National Press Trust (NPT) control the newspapers of Pakistan?
subjective.answer: The National Press Trust was established by Ayub Khan's government in 1964 with the stance that the Trust would look after or take over those newspapers that were suffering from financial crisis or were dangerous to the country's security. Apparently it was an independent body, but actually it was state-controlled. The publications of Progressive Papers Ltd — Pakistan Times, Imroz, Lail-o-Nehar and Sports Times — were handed over to the NPT, and gradually it took over almost 60% of the renowned newspapers of the country, including Daily Mashriq, the Sindhi paper Hilal-e-Pakistan and Morning News. Dawn, Jang and Nawa-i-Waqt were the only major papers not taken into government custody, although they still had a tough time in Ayub's era.
